title: Cast out, but covered
teaser: Before the gate closes behind Adam, God kills to clothe him. The first death in Scripture is God's, for our shame.

modules.hebrewOriginal: וַיַּעַשׂ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם
modules.passage: Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called out to the man, "Where are you?" ... And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

modules.meaning: tunics of skin, garments of hide
modules.rootMeaning: Kuttonet is a long tunic worn against the body. Or means skin or hide - the covering of a living animal. Together: a garment made from a creature that had to die.
modules.usageNote: The same word kuttonet later names the robe Jacob gives Joseph (Genesis 37:3) and the priestly tunics Moses makes for Aaron's sons (Exodus 28:40). The first kuttonet in Scripture is sewn by God Himself, in a garden, over shame.

wordByWord.meaning: the LORD God - the covenant name joined to the Creator name
and He clothed them - He dressed them Himself

relatedWords.reference: Or (skin) sounds almost identical to or (light). A rabbinic reading notes that Adam was first clothed in light, then, after the fall, in skin - the same sound, a different glory.

modules.definition: a tunic; a long shirt-like garment worn next to the skin
modules.usage: The verb vayyalbishem is tender and deliberate: God does not hand them the garments and walk away. He clothes them, the way a parent dresses a child who cannot yet dress themselves.

modules.heading: The First Word After the Fall Is a Question
modules.body:
Genesis 3 ends in the cool of an evening. The fruit has been eaten, the eyes have been opened, and for the first time two people are ashamed of being seen. So they hide among the trees of the garden they were given. And then, in the breeze of the day, footsteps.

Notice what God does first. He does not arrive with a sentence drawn up. He walks, the way one walks when looking for someone, and He calls: "Where are you?" The question is not for God's information; He knows exactly where Adam is crouching. The question is for Adam. It hands the hiding man a chance to come out and speak.

The Hebrew suggests this was not a new sound. The LORD God is described walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, as though evening walks with God had been the rhythm of the place before shame broke it. The first thing the fall steals is the walk. The first thing God does is take the walk anyway, and go looking.
modules.keyInsight: Before the verdict, before the garments, before the gate closes - mercy moves first. The opening move of God toward fallen people is not a sentence but a search.

modules.heading: The Coats in the Hall Closet
modules.body:
When my grandfather was dying he asked, more than once, where his children were. He knew the answer. Two of them were standing at the foot of the bed. He asked anyway, because asking was how he reached for them when words were getting hard to hold.

There is a kind of question that is not really a request for facts. A parent stands in a quiet house and calls a child's name up the stairs, not because the location is a mystery, but because love wants the other person to turn around and answer.

"Where are you?" lands on Adam like that. God is not auditing the garden. He is reaching for the man who has gone quiet, giving him the dignity of stepping out of the bushes on his own feet and speaking for himself - before anything else is said, before any consequence is named.
modules.connectionToTheme: God's first question after the fall is the voice of a Father reaching for a child who has hidden, not a judge demanding an account.

modules.heading: Leaves They Sewed, Skins He Made
modules.body:
Read verse 7 against verse 21 and the whole chapter turns on the difference. In verse 7 the man and woman sew fig leaves into coverings for themselves. In verse 21 the LORD God makes garments of skin and clothes them.

The leaves were what shame could manage on its own: green, quick, and dead by morning. The skins were what only God could give, and they cost something He had to take. An animal that had done nothing wrong dies in the garden so that two who hid can be covered. This is the first death recorded in Scripture, and it is not a punishment falling on the guilty - it is a covering provided for them. Their hands made leaves. His hands made a sacrifice.

This sits at the very front of the Bible on purpose. The whole rest of the story will work out what this one gesture means: that the covering we cannot make for ourselves, God makes at the price of a life.
modules.historicalContext: Genesis stands at the head of the Torah, the foundation Israel read everything else against. By the time these chapters were written down, Israel already knew an altar where animals died so that a sinful people could draw near. Genesis 3:21 lets the reader feel that whole sacrificial world flowing backward to its source: the first death was God covering shame in a garden.
modules.fascinatingFact: Verse 21 is the hinge of the chapter. Verses 22 through 24 record the expulsion - the man is sent out, cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way back. But God clothes them before He drives them out. They walk into the wilderness already wearing what He gave. The exile is real; so is the covering they carry into it.

modules.ancientTruth: God Himself kills an animal in the garden and clothes the shame of Adam and Eve with garments of skin - a covering they could not make, given at the cost of a life.
modules.modernApplication: We are still in the fig-leaf business: the curated image, the kept-up appearance, the careful version of ourselves we let people see. Like leaves, our coverings are real work and they do not last. The covering that holds is the one we receive, not the one we sew.
modules.connectionPoint: What begins with skins in Genesis runs as a thread through the whole of Scripture. Isaiah sings of being clothed with garments of salvation and wrapped in a robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). Paul tells the Galatians that all who were baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with Christ (Galatians 3:27). John sees a great multitude whose robes have been washed white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14). The garden gave the first thread; the cross is where the garment was finally woven.
modules.newTestamentEcho: What the garden hinted, Christ fulfilled. The death that covered Adam was an animal's; the death that covers us is the Lamb of God's, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). At the cross the innocent dies so the guilty may be clothed - the garden's covering, made whole.

modules.prompt: Where are you hiding right now - and what fig leaves have you been sewing to keep from being seen?
additionalQuestions: When you imagine God walking toward you in the cool of the evening, do you hear a sentence coming, or a search? Why?
What in your life are you still trying to cover by your own effort that God is offering to clothe?
What would it mean to step out from the trees and answer the question "Where are you?" honestly today?

modules.prayerText: Lord, thank You for walking still. Thank You that the first word after the fall was a question and not a sentence. Where I have hidden today, find me. Where I have sewn fig leaves, undress me gently. Clothe me again in what only You can give - not the covering I make, but the covering You provided at the cost of the Lamb. Let this be enough for tonight. Amen.

modules.commitment: Today, this is a sabbath day - there is no task to complete. Sit for five quiet minutes and let one phrase hold you: "Where are you," or "He clothed them." Bring God the one thing you have been covering on your own, and ask Him to clothe it.
leavingAtCross: The fig leaves - the image I keep sewing so no one sees what I am ashamed of
The instinct to hide among the trees when I hear God coming
The fear that God walks toward me only to sentence me
receivingFromCross: A covering I did not make and could not earn, given at the cost of a life
The freedom to be found and still be loved
The promise that even when I am sent into the wilderness, I go wearing what God gave
modules.content: Today, this is a sabbath day - there is no task to complete. Sit for five quiet minutes and let one phrase hold you: "Where are you," or "He clothed them." Bring God the one thing you have been covering on your own, and ask Him to clothe it.

forReflection: What is the difference between the fig leaves of verse 7 and the garments of skin of verse 21 - in who makes them, what they cost, and how long they last?
Why does God ask "Where are you?" if He already knows where Adam is?
How does the first death in Scripture, in the garden, point forward to the cross?
forAccountabilityPartners: Name one fig leaf you have been sewing lately - one way you cover so others won't see the real thing.
Talk about what it feels like to be 'found' by God rather than to hide - is it threat, relief, or both?
Ask each other: where is God offering to clothe you in something you have been trying to cover on your own?

relatedScriptures.text: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.
...for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

forDeeperStudy.title: Genesis 3
forDeeperStudy.note: Read the whole chapter slowly, watching the movement from hiding (v. 8) to question (v. 9) to covering (v. 21) to exile (vv. 22-24).

modules.name: Adam
modules.title: The First Man, Clothed by God
modules.description: The first human, formed from the ground and given the garden to keep. After eating the forbidden fruit, Adam hid from God in shame - and was sought, questioned, covered, and only then sent out. He is the head of the human story Scripture says Christ came to redeem: where Adam brought sin and death, the second Adam brings righteousness and life (Romans 5:18-19).
modules.keyQuote: I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.
modules.lessonForUs: Adam's instinct was ours: hide, sew leaves, fear the footsteps. But the God who walked toward him is the God who walks toward us - and the covering He provides still costs Him, and still holds.
modules.heading: The First Man, Clothed by God
